notes: Complete EWCA judgment on case management discretion and actuarial evidence in fatal accident claims.

enrichment.short_title: Fatal accident appeal: district judge wrongly ordered joint actuary where multiplier dispute was mainly legal not actuarial
key_facts: Mrs Prigmore died in a road traffic accident leaving a husband and dependants including Claire, a disabled 14-year-old daughter requiring lifelong care.
The main financial dispute concerned the multiplicand (£30,000–£40,000 v £10,000 p.a.) and the period of dependency, not actuarial calculation.

At a CMC the district judge ordered a single joint actuary to calculate multipliers; the defendants appealed, contending most of the £60,000–£70,000 difference arose from the legal question whether multipliers run from date of death or date of trial.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal with permission against a district judge's case management order at the Sheffield District Registry.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; order for a single joint actuarial report rescinded and discretion re-exercised against actuarial evidence.
enrichment.ratio: Where the substantial multiplier difference in a fatal accident claim reflects the legal issue of Cookson v Knowles date-of-death calculation versus Ogden trial-date methodology rather than actuarial complexity, and the multiplicand is disputed, a case management judge exceeds the permissible discretion in ordering joint actuarial evidence; involvement of the Court of Protection does not itself justify an actuary.
legal_issues: Whether actuarial evidence was necessary for multiplier calculation in a complex fatal accident claim
Distinction between questions of legal principle and questions of actuarial calculation
Scope of appellate interference with case management discretion
Relevance of Court of Protection involvement to expert directions

enrichment.short_title: House builders' judicial review of North West RPG13 fails on legitimate expectation and procedural fairness

statutes_considered.title: Town and Country Planning (Development Plan) (England) Regulations 1999

key_facts: JS Bloor and other North West Housing and Land Consortium members challenged RPG13 issued on 31 March 2003, targeting policies SD4 (North Cheshire), UR7 (housing provision), UR4 (land recycling targets) and DP1 (economy in use of land).

After the public examination panel reported in 2001, the Secretary of State published revised draft RPG in May 2002 with major new policies; HLC sought reconvening of the panel but the Secretary of State proceeded to final RPG13 after written consultation.
Claimants argued breach of legitimate expectation, departure from PPG11, procedural unfairness, inadequate reasons on UR4, and irrational inconsistency in DP1.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Claim for judicial review of the Secretary of State's issue of Regional Planning Guidance for the North West (RPG13).
enrichment.ratio: PPG11 does not create a legitimate expectation that major post-panel changes to draft RPG will be reconsidered by an independent panel; the Secretary of State may make significant changes after written consultation without reopening the public examination, and policies DP1, UR4 and UR8 can be read together without inconsistency.
legal_issues: Whether PPG11 gave rise to a legitimate expectation of panel reconvening for major post-panel policy changes
Whether failure to reopen the public examination was procedurally unfair or irrational
Adequacy of reasons for increased recycling targets in policy UR4
Whether policy DP1 conflicted irrationally with UR4 and UR8

enrichment.short_title: Open-gear beam trawlers: High Court refers EU days-at-sea restrictions to Court of Justice for validity ruling

statutes_considered.title: Sea Fishing (Restriction on Days at Sea) Order 2003

key_facts: Unitymark Ltd operates North Sea open-gear beam trawlers targeting flatfish with minimal cod by-catch compared with cod-targeted and Nephrops vessels.
Council Regulation 2341/2002 and the 2003 UK Order restricted days at sea by gear type, allocating fewer days to beam trawlers than to many other fleets despite their lower cod impact.

Claimants accepted cod conservation was urgent but contended the scheme was disproportionate and discriminatory; the court could not declare EU measures invalid and had to refer if not completely confident of validity.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Judicial review of the Sea Fishing (Restriction on Days at Sea) Order 2003, with application for reference to the Court of Justice on validity of the underlying EU measures.
enrichment.outcome: Reference to the Court of Justice ordered on proportionality and discrimination; costs reserved.
enrichment.ratio: A national court other than a court of last resort must refer questions of validity of EU legislation unless it can resolve them with complete confidence; where open-gear beam trawlers bear the heaviest days-at-sea restrictions despite the smallest cod by-catch, the court could not be completely confident the Regulation and Commission Decision were valid.
legal_issues: Whether Annex XVII days-at-sea restrictions were disproportionate to cod conservation objectives
Whether the scheme unlawfully discriminated against open-gear beam trawlers
When a national court must refer validity questions to the Court of Justice
Margin of appreciation of Community institutions in common fisheries policy measures

enrichment.short_title: Construction adjudicator lacked jurisdiction where battle of forms left existence of written contract genuinely disputed

statutes_considered.title: Housing Grants, Construction and Regeneration Act 1996
Scheme for Construction Contracts (England and Wales) Regulations 1998

key_facts: Pegram Shopfitters carried out Oxford Street refurbishment works for Tally Weijl in 2000 amid a battle of forms between the claimant's standard conditions and the defendant's JCT Prime Cost Contract 1998.
An adjudicator appointed under the statutory Scheme awarded £115,015.50; the defendant participated under protest denying jurisdiction.
The TCC judge gave summary judgment enforcing the award, precluding the defendant's alternative case that if JCT terms did not apply there was no written construction contract at all.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Technology and Construction Court summary judgment enforcing an adjudicator's decision under CPR Part 24.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; judge's order set aside.
enrichment.ratio: On enforcement of an adjudicator's decision, a defendant with a realistic arguable case that there was no agreement in writing within section 107 HGCRA—or that the Scheme did not apply because the contract was on JCT terms—is not estopped from raising that jurisdictional objection merely because it also contended for a different contract; uncertainty over incorporated terms is not a shortcut to Scheme jurisdiction.
legal_issues: Whether a construction contract in writing existed for HGCRA Part II purposes
Which adjudication procedure applied after a battle of forms
Whether the adjudicator could decide contractual formation and his own jurisdiction
Limits of 'pay now, argue later' in adjudication enforcement

enrichment.short_title: Asylum seeker's late permission appeal refused despite arguable procedural flaws in warrant verification
key_facts: Nepalese Maoist claimant Pant arrived in 1997, was refused asylum, lost before an adjudicator in July 1999 and before the IAT in April 2000, but did not seek permission to appeal until February 2003.
She blamed solicitor failings for not receiving the IAT determination, though benefit cessation in 2000 and long inaction weakened her explanation.
Merits arguments focused on failure to adjourn for Home Office verification of arrest warrants and inadequate findings on document authenticity.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Application for permission to appeal to the Court of Appeal against an Immigration Appeal Tribunal decision, out of time.
enrichment.ratio: Very lengthy unexplained delay in seeking permission to appeal will ordinarily defeat an application even where there are unsatisfactory features in the asylum decision; outstanding Article 3 human rights claims do not give equivalent status to a timely asylum appeal and cannot outweigh culpable delay absent exceptional circumstances.
legal_issues: Whether delay of almost three years should be excused
Whether merits of the underlying asylum claim were strong enough to extend time
Propriety of refusing adjournment for verification of arrest warrants
Burden of proof on authenticity of supporting documents

enrichment.short_title: Three-year cap on late VAT input tax deductions upheld under Sixth Directive and Human Rights Act

statutes_considered.title: Human Rights Act 1998
provisions: Schedule 1, Part II, Article 1 First Protocol

key_facts: LAMIT, trustee for property funds opting to tax rents, discovered after changing to cash accounting in 2001 that it had failed to claim £144,308.33 input tax for 1998 accounting periods.
It submitted a voluntary disclosure in November 2001, more than three years after the relevant return deadlines; Customs refused the 1998 claims as time-barred under reg. 29(1A).
LAMIT argued the limit was unauthorised by Article 18(3), disproportionate, breached Rewe equivalence/effectiveness principles, and infringed Article 1 Protocol 1.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal on a point of law from the VAT and Duties Tribunal under section 11(1) Tribunals and Inquiries Act 1992.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal dismissed; three-year limitation on late input tax claims upheld.
enrichment.ratio: Article 18(3) of the Sixth VAT Directive authorises Member States to impose reasonable time limits on late input tax deductions; a three-year cap applied generally to VAT deduction claims satisfies legal certainty and does not breach equivalence, effectiveness or Article 1 Protocol 1 where the claimant could have discovered errors earlier.
legal_issues: Whether reg. 29(1A) validly implemented Articles 17 and 18 of the Sixth Directive
Whether a three-year limit was reasonable and proportionate under Rewe principles
Whether the limit breached the principle of equivalence
Whether denial of recovery infringed peaceful enjoyment of possessions under Article 1 Protocol 1

enrichment.short_title: Turkish pay-TV licence: clause 17 termination payments triable as penalties for failing to credit reverted film rights
key_facts: Cine 5 held a UIP/Studios pay-TV licence for Turkish-language films; after Turkish lira collapse it defaulted on fees and failed to maintain standby letters of credit.
UIP terminated under clause 17 seeking accelerated future licence fees, the full AB Amount (£4.8m advertising/barter pot), reversion of film rights, damages and enforcement costs.
Following termination the Studios also claimed damages for loss of separate five-year renewal options in clause 10.B.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from Commercial Court summary judgment enforcing UIP's termination monetary claims; limited permission on penalty clause and lost-options issues.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed in part: trial ordered on whether clause 17 payments (especially AB Amount and accelerated fees) are unenforceable penalties; summary judgment on lost Studio options upheld; prior litigation costs provision held not penal.
enrichment.ratio: A termination clause requiring payment of future licence fees and the full AB Amount without crediting the licensor's recovered proprietary value in reverted film licences may be penal because actual loss on termination must be assessed as a net balance; a contractual obligation to pay prior litigation costs foregone as part of settlement is a legitimate commercial condition, not a penalty for breach.
legal_issues: Whether clause 17 acceleration and AB Amount provisions were penalty clauses
Whether clause 17 could be severed if part was penal
Whether Studios' renewal options survived UIP's termination
Whether Studios failed to mitigate by not exercising options before termination

notes: Complete case-stated appeal on Food Safety Act prosecution time limits.

enrichment.short_title: Wire in bread roll: prosecution time began when complaint disclosed material facts, not when analyst confirmed manufacturing defect
key_facts: On 15 February 2001 Mr Shah bought baps from Tesco Harrow and found wire embedded in a roll.
On 19 February he telephoned Harrow environmental health; officer Le Brun spoke to Mrs Shah and recorded the complaint but did not see the product until 23 February.
Prosecution was laid on 21 February 2002; magistrates held discovery had not occurred by 19 February, but the Divisional Court held discovery was earlier than 23 April analyst report.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal by case stated from magistrates' conviction of Tesco Stores Ltd for selling food not complying with food safety requirements.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; conviction and sentence quashed; defendant's costs order made.
enrichment.ratio: Under section 34(b) Food Safety Act 1990 'discovery' means disclosure to the prosecutor of facts giving reasonable grounds to believe an offence may have been committed, not completion of investigative verification; the 19 February complaint sufficiently disclosed the material facts and started the one-year period, so prosecution after 21 February 2002 was time-barred.
legal_issues: Meaning of 'discovery by the prosecutor' in section 34(b)
Whether seeing the contaminated product or analyst confirmation was required
Whether poor quality of initial information prevented time running

notes: Complete EWCA judgment on employment bonus construction and change-of-position restitution defence.

enrichment.short_title: Banker's June 2000 bonus letter varied £250k guarantee to £265k; change-of-position defence failed on mistaken overpayment
key_facts: Commerzbank employed investment banker Price-Jones on a February 2000 contract guaranteeing £250,000 bonuses for 2000 and 2001 performance years.
A June 2000 'lock-in' letter during merger rumours offered £265,000 for 2000 paid by March 2001; the bank paid £250,000 in December 2000 by mistake and £265,000 in March 2001.
Price-Jones claimed the 2001 bonus while retaining the December overpayment; the bank sought restitution and set-off.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal from deputy High Court judge's judgment awarding Price-Jones £250,000 and rejecting the bank's restitution/set-off defence.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; June 2000 letter construed as substituting not supplementing the 2000 bonus; change-of-position defence rejected; bank entitled to set off mistaken payment against 2001 bonus.
enrichment.ratio: Reading February and June 2000 letters together, the June letter objectively varied the 2000 guaranteed minimum bonus from £250,000 to £265,000 rather than adding a further payment; retaining a mistaken overpayment cannot be defended by change of position where the recipient's decision to stay was based on his own erroneous interpretation not induced by the payer and he remains enriched.
legal_issues: Construction of guaranteed bonus letters in investment banking employment contract
Whether December 2000 payment was mistaken overpayment recoverable in restitution
Availability of change-of-position defence where reliance preceded receipt
Whether decision to remain with employer constituted disenrichment

enrichment.short_title: SEND Tribunal decision quashed for failing to explain rejection of expert evidence on autistic child's school progress
key_facts: Six-year-old G with autistic spectrum disorder attended a maintained special day school under a statement of SEN; his mother sought LEA funding for a home-based LOVAAS/ABA programme.

Educational psychologist Ms Burgess reported G was not benefiting from the school approach and needed intensive behavioural teaching; the LEA relied on annual review reports and P scale scores showing progress.
The SEND Tribunal dismissed the appeal but gave insufficient reasons for preferring P scale evidence over the mother's and expert evidence on lack of progress.
enrichment.procedural_posture: Appeal to High Court on a point of law against Special Educational Needs and Disability Tribunal decision dismissing appeal against statement contents.
enrichment.outcome: Appeal allowed; Tribunal decision quashed and remitted to a fresh panel; LEA ordered to pay costs.
enrichment.ratio: A SEND Tribunal must deal in its reasons with substantial points raised, expressly explain rejection of expert evidence where relied upon, and where using specialist expertise give parties opportunity to comment; concluding adequate progress from P scales without addressing expert criticism of their significance or accuracy is an error of law.
legal_issues: Adequacy of Tribunal reasons on central issue of progress at named school
Whether rejection of educational psychologist evidence required explicit reasoning
Use of P scale scores versus parental and expert evidence
Duty to put Tribunal expertise to parties before relying on it
